subject: Censoring with an Ordered Logit Model

messages.author: 7d2a96af532ed7de
messages.subject: Censoring with an Ordered Logit Model
parts:
Dear List,

Thanks for Stan!

I'm trying to set up an Ordered Logit of lifetimes (discrete years, 1,2,...,K). Observational units are 'born' at different times. The data has right censoring; plenty of my observations have yet to 'die', but I know how far they've made it to date.

I've rather verbosely described my failed efforts below, but can anyone think of a sensible way of specifying this kind of model?

Apologies if this has come up before (I had a good search, but I'm a bit lost).

Brendan

-----------------

If it's of interest, here's a journey through my failings:

I understand from an error message ("lower truncation not defined for specified arguments to ordered_logistic") that I can't just whack T[L,U] on ordered_logit() for censored data, and build a specification like that in the Estimating Censored Values model on p. 44 (sec 9.2) of the manual.

My second strategy was to set up something like the Ordered Probit model (p. 55), swapping Phi for inv_logit. But for the censored data model, putting a lower bound on eta (based on the current cutpoint estimates), a bit like this:

    data {
        int<lower=0> N_obs;                 // Number of full observations
        int<lower=0> N_cen;                 // Number of right censored observations
        int<lower=2> K;                     // Number of cateogries
        int<lower=1,upper=K> y_obs[N_obs];  // The uncensored data
        real x_obs[N_obs];                  // x for full obs
        real x_cen[N_cen];                  // x for censored obs
        int<lower=1> L_ind[N_cen];          // Vector of current lifetimes (years, so far)
    }
    parameters {
        real beta;
        ordered[K-1] c;
        int<lower=1,upper=K> y_cen[N_cen];
    }
    model {
        vector[K] theta;
        vector[N_cen] L_cut;
       
        for (nc in 1:N_cen) //Define lower bounds in lp units
            L_cut[nc] <- if_else(L_ind[nc] > 1, c[L_ind[nc]-1], -Inf);
       
        for (no in 1:N_obs) {
            real eta;
            eta <- x_obs[no] * beta;
            theta[1] <- 1 - inv_logit(eta - c[1]);
            for (k in 2:(K-1))
                theta[k] <- inv_logit(eta - c[k-1]) - inv_logit(eta - c[k]);
            theta[K] <- inv_logit(eta - c[K-1]);
            y_obs[no] ~ categorical(theta);
        }
       
        for (nc in 1:N_cen) {
            real<lower=L_cut[nc]> eta;
            eta <- x_cen[nc] * beta;
            theta[1] <- 1 - inv_logit(eta - c[1]);
            for (k in 2:(K-1))
                theta[k] <- inv_logit(eta - c[k-1]) - inv_logit(eta - c[k]);
            theta[K] <- inv_logit(eta - c[K-1]);
            y_cen[nc] ~ categorical(theta);
        }
    }

But of course y_cens is int, and as such, can't be modelled as a parameter in Stan (as far as I understand). Changing it to real just to see what would happen, an error message tells me that eta cannot be constrained, which confuses me a bit.

My third strategy was to set up something along the lines of the other censored data model (Integrating out Censored Values, p. 45), where the model is fit on observations, and then lp__ is updated.

However, I can't quite figure out what the appropriate manipulation of lp__ is (or how these manipulations work when I see them on the list!). In short, I've reached the limit of my dire understanding.

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: Censoring with an Ordered Logit Model
parts:
On Thursday, August 15, 2013 12:01:30 PM UTC-4, Brendan wrote:
I'm trying to set up an Ordered Logit of lifetimes (discrete years, 1,2,...,K). Observational units are 'born' at different times. The data has right censoring; plenty of my observations have yet to 'die', but I know how far they've made it to date.

I've rather verbosely described my failed efforts below, but can anyone think of a sensible way of specifying this kind of model?

Can you explain to us why you are inclined to use an ordered logit model for these data? The ordered logit model estimates unknown cutpoints. In your case (and many situations with survival analysis) you know the cutpoints (when a year changes over) and know that they are equally spaced. So, it would seem that you need a count model, rather than an ordinal one. That is still going to be difficult in Stan due to the difficulties with discrete unknowns but easier than trying to do it with an ordinal model.

Ben

messages.author: 7d2a96af532ed7de
messages.subject: Re: Censoring with an Ordered Logit Model
parts:
Cheers for the quick response Ben!

Point taken with the count data. My main inferential interest is the probability that a new unit 'dies' in the next year, so my thought process started with a logit. I'm also trying to build my intuition with Stan ahead of data coming in, by trying lots of specifications with synthetic data. So, I'm afraid the answer to your question is 'No' :) .

A Poisson type model with some allowance for overdispersion is a very good idea. I've tried to get at it in a couple of ways, the least awful is below.

I took the approach used in Gelman & Hill (p. 382) for overdispersion in BUGS, with Gaussian noise on the linear predictor passed to the Poisson distribution function, and the lp__ incrementing method for censored data in the manual (p. 45),

model {
    mu ~ normal(0, 100);
    beta ~ normal(0, 100);
   
    for(n in 1:N_obs)
        lambada_obs[n] ~ normal(mu + x_obs[n] * beta,  sigma);

    y_obs ~ poisson_log(lambada_obs);
   
    for(n in 1:N_cen)
        lambada_cen[n] ~ normal(mu + x_cen[n] * beta,  sigma);

    lp__ <- lp__ + N_cen * log1m(poisson_cdf(L, lambada_cen));
}


...where L (int <lower=0> L[N_cen]) is the lower bounds on the censored data. My intuition is that I should be exponentiating the linear predictor before I pass it to the poisson_cdf, but Stan doesn't like the ways I've tried, and either terminates the R session or throws out of bounds errors.

Confusingly, it seems to estimate mu okay (with enough iterations), but seems to estimate beta and sigma very low. The estimate of beta gets lower as the proportion of censored data gets higher, stepping over 2 SDs away from both the parameter in the data generating mechanism, and the point estimate from a 'full obs only' model when censoring's ~50% of data on a toy problem. When the proportion of censored data is relatively modest (~11%), beta looks okay, but sigma is low,  > 2 SDs away from the 'obs only' estimate, and the parameter in the DGM.

So, the specification above performs worse than an 'obs only' model on the same data set.

Any ideas on where I've gone wrong?

Shouldn't that last line be:

for (n in 1:N_cen)
lp__ <- lp__ + log1m(poisson_cdf(L[n],lambda_cen[n]));

That is, it's the ccdf function you want vectorized.


log Poisson_CCDF(L,lambda_cen)

= SUM_n log Poisson_CCDF(L[n],lambda_cen[n])

= SUM_n log1m(Poisson_CDF(L[n], lambda_cen[n]);

What you have is:

log(1 - SUM_n log poisson_CDF(L[n], lambda_cen[n]);

- Bob

Cheers Bob!

And thanks for taking time to explain how the statements are evaluating.

That's much more intuitive. I'm guessing that the model in the manual (p. 45) works because there's no predictors. It would have taken me a long while to figure out where the implicit summing happens (I'm still getting my head around manipulating lp__ directly).

If it's helpful to anyone searching the list, the above modification produces something that works as expected (in Stan 1.3.0).

Thanks!
